newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians to elect new reformist parliament.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians to elect new reformist parliament.

text.p: Bulgarians vote on Saturday in elections expected to bring to power the former opposition Union of Democratic Forces whose protest campaign toppled the ex-communist Socialists in February.
The election campaign has been something of an anti-climax after the rallies which drew thousands of people every day at the beginning of the year.
Unlike Bulgaria's two previous parliamentary elections since the end of one-party rule, this time the question is not who will win, but by how large a majority.

"On Saturday we must continue what we started in January. Then we were together and now we'll be together again, with one common aim -- to save Bulgaria," UDF leader Ivan Kostov told a rally in the town of Plovdiv on Wednesday.

Kostov can also capitalise on the success of the interim cabinet, which brought the country back from the brink of bankruptcy, negotiating a reform and funding accord with the IMF which has opened the door to credits from other lenders.
"Our election programme is realistic, it is an unique one as it has been already tested by the actions of the caretaker cabinet in an extremely difficult situation," Kostov said.
"Europe and the world decided to invest billions of dollars in the new government of the country. For us this is an investment of confidence which we are determined to maintain."

Opinion polls show the UDF winning up to 60 percent of votes and the Socialists around 20 percent. Three smaller coalitions are also expected to poll above the four percent minimum to enter parliament.

Popular interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski will return to his previous job as mayor of Sofia, and Kostov, an economist by training and former UDF finance minister, is expected to be prime minister.
Several ministers from the interim cabinet are likely to stay on.
Exiled King Simeon visited on Tuesday and Wednesday and urged the country's political forces to unite in a broad coalition to carry out the long-delayed reforms.
After former communist leader Todor Zhivkov was toppled in 1989, leading communists renamed their party the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) and continued in government.
The UDF won parliamentary elections in 1991, but lost a no-confidence vote the following year.

The Socialists won the next election in 1994, but their support evaporated as the economy weakened and a sea-change began with Petar Stoyanov's decisive defeat of the Socialist candidate in presidential elections last year.
The party has now distanced itself from former party leader and prime minister Zhan Videnov, who stepped down in December, and say they have learned from their mistakes.
"The BSP's two-year term in office showed that such severe reform cannot be carried out by a single political force," Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov told the party daily Douma.
"The appeal for national consensus is not an abstract idea. It should unite all those who have a real desire and readiness to implement a policy of reform at an acceptable social price."
The lev currency which went into freefall at the beginning of the year has now stabilised but annual inflation was 2,040.5 percent in March.
Unemployment reached 14.5 percent and is expected to rise further as the government finally tackles closures and restructuring of loss-making state enterprises.
The new government is already committed to reforms agreed with the IMF, including introducing a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime in June to restore monetary stability.
Bulgaria stands to receive credits totalling $1.2 billion from the IMF, European Union and others, most of which must go straight back to lenders as payment on its foreign debt.
